lesson.title: Not Every Gene, All the Time: How Bacteria Control Gene Expression
lesson.summary: Prokaryotic cells regulate which genes are transcribed at any given moment, mainly by controlling whether RNA polymerase can access a gene's promoter, so that they make only the proteins they currently need.
lesson.body:
A bacterial genome carries genes for far more proteins than any single cell needs to make at any given moment. Producing every protein all the time, regardless of whether it is useful, would waste enormous amounts of energy and raw material. Instead, cells regulate gene expression: they turn genes on when their products are needed and off when they are not, in response to changing conditions such as which nutrients are available or what stress the cell is under.

In prokaryotic cells, this regulation happens overwhelmingly at the level of transcription, the process introduced earlier by which RNA polymerase builds an mRNA copy of a gene. Because prokaryotic cells have no nucleus, transcription and translation are not separated in time or space the way they are in eukaryotic cells; a bacterial ribosome can begin translating an mRNA while RNA polymerase is still transcribing the far end of the same gene. That coupling makes controlling transcription itself, whether RNA polymerase is allowed to bind a gene's promoter and begin making mRNA in the first place, an efficient and immediate way to control how much protein gets made, without needing the additional layers of control that eukaryotic cells, with their separate nucleus and more complex genome packaging, rely on.

Bacterial transcriptional control generally works through one of two logical strategies, often used together. Negative control relies on a repressor protein that binds directly to a regulatory DNA sequence near a gene's promoter and physically blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing it; for the gene to be expressed, the repressor must first be removed. Positive control relies on an activator protein that must bind DNA near a promoter to help RNA polymerase transcribe it efficiently; without the activator, transcription happens only weakly or not at all. Both strategies let a single small molecule inside the cell, by binding to the regulatory protein and changing its shape, indirectly switch a gene on or off.

Bacteria very often regulate several genes together rather than one at a time, especially when those genes encode enzymes that work in the same metabolic pathway. Grouping such genes under one shared regulatory switch, an arrangement called an operon, lets the cell turn on an entire pathway's worth of enzymes at once, with a single regulatory decision, rather than needing to regulate each gene separately. That arrangement is the subject of the next chapter.
